meta.name: Breech Delivery — Complete Breech, Hands-Off Technique

history.hpi: G2P1 at 38 weeks gestation presents with regular contractions 2 minutes apart for the last hour and a strong urge to push. Prenatal ultrasound at 36 weeks noted breech presentation; external cephalic version was scheduled but labor began before the appointment. Membranes ruptured 30 minutes ago with clear fluid. Patient reports feeling something firm and rounded at the vaginal opening, not the baby's head.
pastMedical: Uncomplicated first pregnancy/vaginal delivery 3 years ago
history.events: Contractions intensified over the last hour; husband called 911 when patient felt an urge to push and could feel the baby's buttocks at the vaginal opening

scene.location: Second-floor bedroom, patient on bed in left lateral position per husband's instruction from the OB triage nurse line
scene.bystanders: Husband present, on phone with OB triage nurse who advised him to call 911 immediately due to concern for breech presentation
visualCues: Buttocks and both feet visible at vaginal opening (complete breech)
Clear amniotic fluid staining on bedding
Patient gripping bedrails with strong expulsive urge
No visible umbilical cord at introitus

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 26-year-old G2P1 female at 38 weeks with complete breech presentation — buttocks and both feet visible at the vaginal opening — with strong contractions and an uncontrollable urge to push.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Nonlabored between contractions, breath-holding with pushing, 22/min
otherFindings: Complete breech presentation — buttocks and both feet visible at introitus
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I have to push, it's coming, please help me!"

transitions.if: Buttocks and trunk allowed to deliver spontaneously
transitions.condition: Crew recognizes complete breech presentation, positions mother supine, and allows the buttocks, feet, and trunk to deliver spontaneously without traction per protocol.

phases.name: Buttocks and trunk delivered hands-off
phases.description: The buttocks, feet, and trunk deliver spontaneously with the mother's own pushing effort. Crew supports the body without pulling, checks for a prolapsed cord, and prepares to assist head delivery.
phases.triggerCondition: After allowing the presenting buttocks and legs to deliver on their own without traction, the trunk delivers spontaneously with maternal pushing; crew now supports the body and assesses for cord involvement before the head delivers.

otherFindings: Buttocks, both legs, and trunk delivered spontaneously
Fetal trunk supported without traction, kept elevated off any cord
Head remains undelivered, chin tucked toward chest
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Is the baby okay? I can't stop pushing!"

expectedActions.shortAction: Allow buttocks, feet, and trunk to deliver spontaneously without traction
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Place mother supine, allow the buttocks, feet, and trunk to deliver spontaneously, then support the body while the head is delivered
expectedActions.rationale: Traction on a breech fetus before spontaneous descent risks nuchal arm entrapment and cervical injury.

expectedActions.shortAction: Assess for prolapsed cord after trunk delivers
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Assess for presence of prolapsed cord and treat as above
expectedActions.rationale: Cord compression during breech delivery is a leading cause of fetal hypoxia.

expectedActions.shortAction: Support fetal body without traction; keep fetus elevated off the umbilical cord
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Once the legs are delivered support the body to avoid hyperextension of the head; keep the fetus elevated off the umbilical cord... NEVER pull on the body, especially a preterm or previable baby – just support the baby's body while mother pushes when she feels the urge to
expectedActions.rationale: Pulling on the body or letting the fetus hang below the introitus can compress the cord or hyperextend the head.

transitions.condition: The head does not descend spontaneously within moments, so crew performs the protocol's head-entrapment maneuver to open the airway and complete delivery.
Instead of allowing spontaneous descent, the crew pulls on the fetal trunk to hasten delivery, extending the arms above the head and obstructing further descent.

phases.name: Head delivered with jaw-flexion support
phases.description: The head fails to deliver spontaneously after a brief pause, so the crew inserts a gloved hand to flex the fetal neck and create an airway, then completes delivery of the head.
phases.triggerCondition: Because the head does not descend spontaneously immediately after trunk delivery, crew performs the protocol's head-entrapment maneuver — a gloved hand forming a V on the fetal cheeks to flex the chin toward the chest — successfully delivering the head.

otherFindings: Fetal head delivered using gloved-hand jaw-flexion maneuver
Newborn crying vigorously immediately after head delivery
No suctioning performed — airway clear without obstruction

expectedActions.shortAction: Insert gloved hand, form a V with index/ring fingers on fetal cheeks to flex chin to chest and open airway
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If head fails to deliver, place gloved hand into vagina with fingers between infant's face and uterine wall to create an open airway. Place your index and ring fingers on the baby's cheeks forming a "V" taking care not to block the mouth and allowing the chin to be tilted toward the chest flexing the neck
expectedActions.rationale: Flexing the chin opens a passive airway and prevents suffocation while the head remains undelivered.

expectedActions.shortAction: Do not routinely suction the newborn's airway, even with a bulb syringe
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Do not routinely suction the infant's airway (even with a bulb syringe) during delivery
expectedActions.rationale: Routine suctioning can cause vagal bradycardia and is not shown to improve outcomes.

transitions.condition: Newborn is delivered completely, dried, warmed, and placed skin-to-skin; crew prepares for cord clamping and transport.

phases.name: Newborn dried, warmed, and stabilized
phases.description: The newborn is delivered completely, dried, warmed, and stimulated with good cry and color. Cord is clamped after 1 minute; APGAR is scored; mother and newborn are packaged for transport.
phases.triggerCondition: With a vigorous, crying newborn and no signs of maternal hemorrhage, crew completes routine post-delivery care and prepares both patients for transport.

otherFindings: Newborn pink, crying vigorously, active motion of all extremities — APGAR 9 at 1 minute
Cord clamped and cut after 1-minute delay
Fundus firm at umbilicus, minimal vaginal bleeding
Placenta not yet delivered — not forced, contained if passed

expectedActions.shortAction: Dry, warm, and stimulate newborn; place skin-to-skin on maternal chest
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Dry, warm, and stimulate infant, wrap in towel and place on maternal chest unless resuscitation needed
expectedActions.rationale: Newborns lose heat rapidly and stimulation promotes respiratory effort.

expectedActions.shortAction: Clamp cord ~5-6 inches from abdomen after a 1-minute delay, then cut between clamps
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: After 1 minute, clamp cord about 5–6 inches from the abdomen with two clamps; cut the cord between the clamps
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed cord clamping improves neonatal blood volume and iron stores.

expectedActions.shortAction: Record APGAR score at 1 and 5 minutes once neonate is stabilized
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Record APGAR scores at 1 and 5 minutes once neonate is stabilized
expectedActions.rationale: APGAR scoring standardizes neonatal status communication to the receiving facility.

phases.name: Traction applied to speed delivery
phases.description: Instead of allowing the breech to deliver hands-off, the crew pulls on the fetal trunk to hasten delivery. This extends the arms above the head (nuchal arm entrapment), obstructing further delivery and risking cervical spine injury and fetal hypoxia.
phases.triggerCondition: Anxious about a prehospital breech delivery, the crew pulls on the fetal trunk instead of allowing spontaneous descent, causing the arms to extend above the head and obstructing further delivery.

otherFindings: Fetal arm(s) extended above the head, delivery obstructed
No further descent despite continued maternal pushing
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Something's wrong, it's not coming out anymore!"

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize obstructed delivery from traction; rotate fetal trunk to free the extended arm(s), then resume hands-off support
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: When delivering breech, you may need to rotate the baby's trunk clockwise; or sweep the legs from the vagina
expectedActions.rationale: Rotating the trunk can free an entrapped arm caused by premature traction, restoring progress toward delivery.
